title: Dances at the school with Buddy Petit
summary: He recalls playing for years at neighbourhood dances including a school hall, with Buddy Petit, and remembers trombonist Joe Plessy.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Yeah, I say the Portuguese people going there.
Oh yeah. Oh well that used to be our home. We used to play there for the, what you call the Tormal Bunch, and the Irish Channel Bunch.

No, this gang of boys get together with their girls, we go out there for them, then we used to play back here, Broad and Tulane. Not Tulane, Street, but after Tulane, before you get to Tulane on this side.
Oh yeah, I know that school.
We played there for years, you know what I mean? Everything come through there, we played it. Everything. You were with Chris Kelly then? No, I was with, we was with Buddy. Buddy Petitia.
They had us, but dances in the school? That's right.

That's right, and that would be twice a month. Oh yeah, that wrist ring up our bones, don't forget. That's when I'm going to be there. I know that, but we couldn't buy that date for nothing. This boy died, Plessy, how they call him, Joe Plessy? I believe he died, he used to play trombone. Yeah, I heard of him. He used to be at our dance all the time. He's supposed to be a nice guy.

Oh man, that's a fine boy. That's fine, trombone. I seen Joe died, you heard that? I believe so. I think I heard it, but I heard that afterwards. I knew them boys, I knew, man, that, uh, I knew if they got away from me, mind me being scattered, but they used to, they'd go, they'd come up, we'd be talking, they'd come up to me. Used to, uh, had the Lucian tenor, we used to play there, then we used to play up in the Irish Channel. Yards up in there, man, at lawn parties. Started playing at eight o'clock, and ended up about six in the morning. You couldn't go when they got you there, but they paid you all right. They treated you all right. Got anything you wanted, more than what you could handle. More than you could handle, and you were treated for each class. But you couldn't go, you had to stay there and play. But I didn't mean, uh, just keep playing, you know, play on this like your regular time of playing. White and black was the same thing, because you gave up all the here. You played for white, when you look up, there's much black as they had white. You played over there for white, and you got there as much black as they had white. All they want is don't you touch it either. Don't interfere with it. You know, the Irish Channel used to be tough up there. No policeman didn't go up there. You go up there, you had to go up there like a gentleman with his hat in his hand. There'd be a fight between them. You two fight, go ahead and fight. You have to fight. No knife, no gun or nothing. This state ain't fight. See when he got whipsy, oh that's all I gotta know. Shake hands. Let's go to this. Now they don't want to hear that no more. Don't want to hear it no more. They'll come up there, you my buddy, beat my friend up and all that. Uh-uh. You want to fight? Play and fight. That's the way it was. I remember one time we played at the lake. I'll never forget this as long as I've been. Uh, this boy, Edward Gasper was playing drums and that boy used to keep a beautiful set of drums. I knew him, dumb man, was a, oh, really beautiful. So, uh, somehow or another, we were playing that food at the Donate at the, uh, Spanish Food. Well, our camp went down the run and our camp set off this run. Another run, the run down there, the other camp come in this. That they make the boot of the band fight each other right from the back. You know man, we played over, I don't know if it was shocking them or who it was, I can't just remember. But when we got there, we had a habit, we test the band out. See, we tune with the band out, we had a band over there, man, we bust loose and running about three or four hard numbers. Man, they get hot, they start to bust now. Well, we know how strong it was when they played. It was blow down on them. Man, they get hot, man, they be playing and blowing at us, man. We wouldn't pay them to mind. Now, when they slept, we'd shake them up a little bit. Part of that evening, come on, they all would come up. Their band was better than our band. They left them way around then, come to our camp and save that. Part of when they come there with that, they start all home, they start the free for all. Now, this was the run coming right in here. And all the hall was in the center like this, you know. This was the hall here, the house, and all around here was the gallery. This was the run going through. Man, they started fighting, free for all. All around there, man, I had twice drumming, man. I couldn't get out with it, no way. When I did get out with it, took a run on the run. Man, they fit there, the policeman come there, man. They threw him in the lake. Then the crowd come there, man. I'll never forget the one in there. When we did get away, they settled out. They put a couple of them in jail, man. So the woman we was playing for, she'd come back. She had to run down.
